e.etymology: From Greek Timotheos: timao (to honor) plus theos (god). In the New Testament Timothy is the young companion of Paul addressed in two epistles.
namesakes: Timothy Dalton (actor who played James Bond)

e.etymology: From an English surname, most likely from Anglo-Norman bailli (bailiff, steward); in some families it referred to the bailey, the outer wall of a castle.
namesakes: George Bailey (hero of It's a Wonderful Life)

assoc.t: Baileys Irish Cream liqueur
Barnum and Bailey circus

e.note: Also one of the most popular dog names in the United States.

e.meaning: from Lennox, a district of Scotland; often read as elm grove
e.etymology: From a Scottish surname and earldom, Gaelic Leamhnach, the land along the River Leven, whose name is usually tied to the Gaelic word for elm.

assoc.t: Lennox heating and air conditioning
Lenox china and tableware, spelled with one n

e.etymology: From Hebrew Avraham. Genesis explains it as father of a multitude, the name God gives Abram (exalted father), patriarch of Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

assoc.t: Abraham Lincoln, sixteenth US president
Abraham, patriarch of three major religions

e.etymology: From Old Welsh Morcant, possibly mor (sea) or maur (great) plus cant (circle). A men's name in Wales for centuries, it became unisex in the United States in the 1980s.
namesakes: Morgan le Fay (sorceress of Arthurian legend)

assoc.t: JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley, Wall Street banks
Morgan le Fay, sorceress of Arthurian legend
Captain Morgan spiced rum

e.etymology: From Greek anastasis (resurrection), the name of a fourth-century martyr. Early Christians gave it to children born around Easter, and it is a favorite in Eastern Europe.
namesakes: Grand Duchess Anastasia (youngest daughter of the last Russian tsar)
Anastasia Steele (heroine of Fifty Shades of Grey)

assoc.t: Anastasia, 1997 animated film about the lost princess
Grand Duchess Anastasia Romanov of Russia
Anastasia Beverly Hills cosmetics

e.etymology: A Scottish pet form of Elspeth, the Scots form of Elizabeth (Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath). It has stood on its own since the 1800s.

assoc.t: Elsie the Cow, Borden dairy mascot

e.etymology: The heroine of the 1877 Spanish novel Amaya, set among the Basques, whose author explained it by Basque amai (the end). Amaya is also a village in northern Spain.

e.meaning: from a Scottish place name, probably ditch or muddy place
e.etymology: From the Scottish surname Brodie, taken from the lands of Brodie in Moray, a name usually traced to a Gaelic word for a ditch or mire.
namesakes: Chief Brody (the police chief in Jaws)

e.etymology: A spelling of Catherine, from Greek Aikaterine, of uncertain origin. Early Christians tied it to katharos (pure), which gave the spelling with th. Saint Catherine of Alexandria spread it.
namesakes: Katherine Johnson (NASA mathematician of Hidden Figures)

e.etymology: A modern short form of Alexander, from Greek Alexandros (defender of men). Xander Harris of Buffy the Vampire Slayer helped popularize it in the United States.
namesakes: Xander Harris (Buffy the Vampire Slayer character)

assoc.t: Xander Harris of Buffy the Vampire Slayer

e.etymology: From Greek Adonis, the beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite. The Greek name comes from a Semitic word for lord, like Hebrew adon.
namesakes: Adonis Creed (boxer hero of the Creed films)

assoc.t: Adonis, beautiful youth of Greek myth loved by Aphrodite
an Adonis, a strikingly handsome young man
Adonis Creed, boxer hero of the Creed films

e.note: As an ordinary word, an Adonis is a very handsome man, which is a lot to hang on a child.

e.etymology: From the Late Latin name Victor (conqueror), popular with early Christians and borne by several saints and popes. The English word victor is the same word.

assoc.t: victor, the ordinary word for a winner

e.etymology: From Hebrew Yo'el (Yahweh is God), the name of one of the twelve minor prophets of the Hebrew Bible.
namesakes: Joel Miller (protagonist of The Last of Us)

assoc.t: Joel, the smuggler hero of The Last of Us
Billy Joel, the Piano Man singer, by surname

e.meaning: deer friend (Irish) or god's spear (Old English)
e.etymology: A blend of two names: Irish Oscar, grandson of Fionn mac Cumhaill, read as deer friend, and Old English Osgar (god spear). The Ossian poems of the 1760s revived it and Swedish kings carried it across Europe.

assoc.t: the Oscars, the Academy Awards and their statuette
Oscar the Grouch of Sesame Street
Oscar Mayer hot dogs and lunch meats

e.etymology: From Hebrew Hevel, possibly the word for breath or vapor, or from an Akkadian word for son. In Genesis Abel is the second son of Adam and Eve, killed by his brother Cain.
namesakes: Abel (son of Adam and Eve in Genesis)
Abel Tesfaye (the singer known as The Weeknd)

assoc.t: Abel, slain by his brother in the story of Cain and Abel

e.etymology: Invented by American parents in the 1990s to rhyme with the equally fashionable Aidan, Braden, Hayden and Jayden.
A medieval form of the Latin saint's name Oliva (olive), revived in the 19th century when plant names came into fashion. The olive branch is an old symbol of peace.
namesakes: Olive Kitteridge (title character of the Pulitzer-winning novel)

assoc.t: olive, the fruit, its oil and the drab green color
Olive Oyl, Popeye's girlfriend
Olive Garden, Italian restaurant chain

e.etymology: A Hawaiian word for the orange tree and its fruit. In the United States it also reads as a variant of Alana, and it rose alongside Leilani and other -lani names.

assoc.t: Alani Nu energy drinks, often just called Alani

e.meaning: feminine form of Alan; in Hawaiian, awakening
e.etymology: A feminine form of Alan in regular use since the 20th century. A separate Hawaiian name Alana, from alana (awakening), has reinforced it.
namesakes: Alana Haim (musician in the band Haim and actress)

e.etymology: A Slavic men's name from mil (gracious, dear), common in Czech, Slovak and Serbian. In the United States it is also taken from the Italian city, especially for girls.

assoc.t: Milan, Italy's fashion and design capital
AC Milan and Inter Milan soccer clubs

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, Old English brom (broom shrub) plus dun (hill). It was a leading boys' name in the US and Canada in the 1980s and 1990s.

assoc.t: Let's Go Brandon, 2021 political slogan aimed at Joe Biden

e.note: The 2021 slogan Let's Go Brandon, a coded jab at Joe Biden, still follows the name for some people.

e.etymology: From French Rosalie, the Latin saint's name Rosalia, from rosa (rose). Saint Rosalia is the patron of Palermo.

assoc.t: Rosalie Hale, vampire sister in Twilight

e.etymology: From an English surname based on the Old English personal name Tata, from a Germanic root meaning glad or cheerful; a similar Old Norse name also fed into it.

assoc.t: Andrew Tate, controversial online influencer
Tate galleries, including Tate Modern in London
Tate's Bake Shop cookies

e.etymology: From Hebrew Rut, of uncertain origin, possibly companion. Ruth is the loyal Moabite heroine of the Book of Ruth; Puritans also linked it to the English word ruth (compassion).
namesakes: Ruth (heroine of the biblical Book of Ruth)

assoc.t: Babe Ruth, baseball legend, by surname
Book of Ruth in the Bible
Baby Ruth candy bar

e.etymology: From Old English Eadweard: ead (wealth, fortune) plus weard (guard). One of the few Old English names to survive the Norman Conquest, it was borne by eleven English kings.
namesakes: Edward VIII (British king who abdicated in 1936)

assoc.t: Edward Cullen, the vampire of Twilight

e.etymology: From an Irish surname, Ó Leannáin (descendant of Leannán, lover) and also Ó Lonáin (descendant of Lonán, blackbird). As a first name it honors John Lennon of the Beatles.

assoc.t: John Lennon of the Beatles

e.etymology: From Hebrew Ari'el: ari (lion) plus el (God), a biblical name for Jerusalem. Shakespeare used it for the spirit in The Tempest, and Disney's 1989 Little Mermaid made it a girls' name.

assoc.t: Ariel, Disney's Little Mermaid
Ariel, the spirit in Shakespeare's The Tempest

e.meaning: pet form of Caroline, free woman
e.etymology: From a 19th-century pet form of Caroline, the feminine of Charles (free man). It is also used as a short form of Calista and Calliope.

assoc.t: Cali, nickname for California, by sound

e.etymology: A feminine form of Ariel, from Hebrew ari (lion) plus el (God).
The Latinate feminine of Andreas and Andrew, from Greek aner, andros (man), with the sense manly or brave. In Italy Andrea is the men's form of the name.

e.meaning: feminine form of Brian, probably high or noble
e.etymology: A feminine form of the Irish name Brian, probably from a Celtic root meaning high or noble. The spelling Briana appears in Spenser's The Faerie Queene; wide use dates from the 1980s.
